blocks.title: What ICAI's published papers tell us
bullets: ICAI has not published examiners' comments for Paper 6, so this guidance comes from ICAI's suggested answers, RTPs and MTPs.
SM Chapter 1 appears in **every attempt** from May 2024 to May 2026, usually as one 5-mark descriptive part plus one or two 2-mark MCQs (7–12 marks per paper).

Top areas: **strategic intent** (vision, mission, objectives, values: 10 past-paper items), **proactive vs reactive strategy** (6 items), **importance and limitations of strategic management** (5 items), **strategic levels and networks** (3 items).

Every RTP from Jan 2025 to Sep 2026 carries two Chapter 1 descriptive questions, and the same cases repeat: Vikram Patel's bookstores, Ramesh Sharma's stores, drafting a vision and mission for a new brand, hiring a CEO.

blocks.title: How ICAI answers this chapter (study guidance)
bullets: Case questions carry an **identification mark** (e.g. '1 + 4 marks'): name the concept first (Functional level, Vision, Proactive and reactive), then explain it in study-material words, then apply it to the facts.

ICAI's answers follow the study-material lists closely: seven benefits of strategic management, four limitations, ten characteristics of objectives, seven reasons for a mission, four essentials of a strategic vision, three network relationships.
'Draft a vision and mission' questions are answered with a one-line vision plus **three mission bullets**, each preceded by the SM definition of vision and mission.
Where facts show a firm acting ahead of change **and** adapting to shocks, ICAI's answer is 'partly proactive and partly reactive' (PYQ Jan 2025 MCQ 11, May 2026 MCQ 11).

concepts.title: 1.1–1.2 Introduction; Meaning and Nature of Strategic Management
understand: **Introduction (§1.1).** With increased competition, business management has acquired a **strategic dimension**. All executives and professionals, including **Chartered Accountants**, working towards business growth must possess sound knowledge of strategic management concepts.

Opening quotes in the SM: Michael Porter — "The company without a strategy is willing to try anything." Henry Mintzberg — "Strategy is not the consequence of planning, but the opposite: it's the starting point."

**Management in two senses (§1.2). (a) A key group** in charge of the organisation's affairs: management is the **chief organ** that makes the organisation a purposeful and productive entity by bringing together and integrating the disorganised resources of **manpower, money, material and technology** into a functioning whole. An organisation becomes a unified functioning system when management mobilises and uses these resources efficiently and effectively. Survival and success depend largely on the **competence and character** of management, which must also facilitate **organisational change and adaptation** for effective interaction with the environment.

**(b) A set of interrelated functions and processes** carried out by that key group to attain objectives: **Planning, Organising, Directing, Staffing and Control**. These range from determining goals, designing the organisation, mobilising and acquiring resources, allocating tasks and resources among personnel and activity units, to installing control systems so that what is planned is achieved.

==Management is an influence process to make things happen==, to gain command over phenomena, to induce and direct events and people in a particular manner. Influence is backed by **power, competence, knowledge and resources**. Managers formulate organisational goals, values and strategies to cope with, adapt and adjust to changes in the environment.

==The strategic management process is the set of activities that firm managers undertake to put their firms in the best possible position to compete successfully in the marketplace.== Its distinct activities: **developing the firm's vision and mission; strategic analysis; developing objectives; creating, choosing and implementing strategies; and measuring and evaluating performance**.
concepts.example: When a hospital chain's top team sets a vision, studies competitors and regulations, fixes growth targets, chooses to open telemedicine services, rolls them out and tracks patient numbers, it is running the full strategic management process.
keywords: Planning, Organising, Directing, Staffing and Control
put their firms in the best possible position to compete successfully

concepts.title: 1.3 Concept of Strategy — Strategy Is Partly Proactive and Partly Reactive
concepts.evidence: PYQ 6 (Sep 2024 MCQ 9, Jan 2025 MCQ 11 & Q5(b), Jan 2026 Q8(b) OR, May 2026 MCQ 11 & Q8(b) OR) · RTP 3 · MTP 9
understand: **Meaning.** In business, strategy relates to ==the ways the business decides to respond to dynamic and often hostile external forces while pursuing its vision, mission and ultimate objectives==. Strategy is intended to **unravel complexity and reduce uncertainty** caused by environmental change, and **relates the goals of the organisation to the means of achieving them**.

==Strategy is the game plan that the management uses to take market position, conduct its operations, attract and satisfy customers, compete successfully, and achieve organizational objectives.== (SM MCQ 1 key: all of these.) It is associated with unified design and action for achieving major goals, gaining command over the situation with a **long-range perspective** and securing a **critically advantageous position**.
**Definition:** a **long-range blueprint** of an organisation's desired image, direction and destination: what it wants to be, what it wants to do, how it wants to do things and where it wants to go.

**Igor H. Ansoff:** the common thread among the organisation's activities and product-markets that defines the essential nature of business the organisation has or plans to be in. **William F. Glueck:** a unified, comprehensive and integrated plan designed to assure that the basic objectives of the enterprise are achieved.

Strategy is a consciously considered and **flexibly designed scheme** of corporate intent and action to mobilise resources, direct human effort and behaviour, handle events and problems, perceive and use opportunities, and meet challenges and threats for corporate survival and success. It meets the organisation's need for **dynamic direction, focus and cohesiveness**; objectives alone do not. It provides an integrated framework for top management to search for, evaluate and exploit opportunities, meet threats and crises, use strengths and offset weaknesses.

==Strategy is no substitute for sound, alert and responsible management.== ==Strategy can never be perfect, flawless and optimal== (SM MCQ 2). It is by nature **flexible and pragmatic** to handle emergencies and pressures; allowances are made for miscalculations and unanticipated events.

**Levels:** in large organisations strategies are formulated at the **corporate, divisional and functional** levels. Corporate strategies (by top managers) cover expansion and growth, vertical and horizontal integration, diversification, takeovers and mergers, new investment and divestment areas, R&D projects etc. They are operationalised by divisional and functional strategies on product lines, production volumes, quality ranges, prices, promotion, market penetration, purchasing sources, personnel development and the like.

**Strategy is partly proactive and partly reactive.** A company's strategy is typically a **blend** of (i) ==proactive actions by managers to improve market position and financial performance== and (ii) ==reactions to unanticipated developments and fresh market conditions== in the dynamic environment. ==Proactive strategy is planned strategy, whereas reactive strategy is adaptive reaction to changing circumstances.== (SM MCQ 3: a blend; SM MCQ 4: reactive = adaptive strategy.)

**SM figure:** the latest version of the company's strategy (actual strategy) = **proactive strategy elements** (new initiatives plus ongoing strategy elements continued from prior periods) + **reactive strategy elements** (adaptive reactions to changing circumstances), shaped by company experiences, know-how, resources, strengths, weaknesses and competitive capabilities; some elements are **abandoned**.

The proactive part is the product of management's analysis and strategic thinking about how to position the company. But not every strategic move results from proactive planning: when market or competitive conditions take an unexpected turn, or some aspect of strategy **hits a stone wall**, a strategic reaction or adjustment is required. So strategy is partly a reasoned response to unforeseen developments.

==Crafting a strategy involves stitching together a proactive/intended strategy based on prior successful experience and then adapting pieces of successful reactions as circumstances change or better options emerge (a reactive/adaptive strategy).==

Strategy also means identifying existing problems and solving them by executing revolutionary ideas: **UPI (Unified Payments Interface)** changed India's digital payments landscape and has gone global — a well-planned identification of a problem, formulation of a strategy and perfect execution.

**Is this a strategy? (SM box):** a ketchup brand making healthier ketchup with less sugar and preservatives so parents feel safe — **yes**, a business strategy to fight competition and adapt to a changing external environment (people becoming health conscious).

official_questions.question: Ecro Ltd., an e-commerce company selling eco-friendly products, keeps strengthening its brand identity, launching creative campaigns and introducing innovative eco-friendly products. When large retailers entered the eco-friendly space, it quickly adapted: it analysed competitors' strategies, changed its marketing style in response to their actions and countered their pricing. Discuss the strategic approaches Ecro Ltd. took in the two situations, and explain the strategy it should adopt in future to remain competitive. (1 + 1 + 3 marks)
answer_points: Ecro Ltd. uses both proactive and reactive strategic approaches to stay competitive in a dynamic market.

**Situation 1 — proactive:** strengthening brand identity (a strong eco-friendly image for environmentally conscious consumers); innovative marketing campaigns to enhance visibility and differentiate products; product innovation (new eco-friendly products to meet evolving demands). These are deliberate, planned actions to improve market position and financial performance.

**Situation 2 — reactive:** adapting to market changes (responding to large retailers' entry by quickly adjusting strategies); competitor analysis (studying competitors' strategies to counteract them); dynamic marketing (varied techniques in response to competitors' campaigns); pricing adjustments (counter-pricing without compromising profitability). These show its ability to adapt to unforeseen developments.

**Future strategy — a blended approach:** (1) sustainable differentiation through continuous innovation and exclusive eco-friendly lines; (2) customer-centric approach using data analytics to understand preferences; (3) operational efficiency by optimising the supply chain and reducing costs; (4) strategic alliances with eco-certification organisations to build credibility and trust.
official_questions.conclusion: By integrating planned proactive initiatives with adaptive responses, Ecro Ltd. can navigate uncertainty, tackle competition and ensure long-term success.
official_questions.examiner: No examiners' comments have been published for Paper 6.

official_questions.question: Differentiate between proactive and reactive strategies. Explain in detail why it is important for every organisation to use both in a dynamic and uncertain business environment. (1 + 4 marks)
answer_points: **Meaning:** proactive strategy — planned and deliberate actions taken by management to improve market position and performance; reactive strategy — adaptive responses to unforeseen changes and unexpected developments in the business environment.
**Nature:** proactive is planned and intentional; reactive is responsive and adaptive.
**Objective:** proactive — gain competitive advantage through advance planning; reactive — cope with changing circumstances and environmental uncertainties.

**Why both are needed:** (1) proactive strategies help achieve planned objectives — long-term direction, market position; (2) reactive strategies help cope with uncertainty — unexpected changes in competition, technology, regulations or customer preferences; (3) the combination gives flexibility and adaptability; (4) it ensures survival and competitive advantage — firms can exploit opportunities, tackle threats and handle crises in turbulent environments.
official_questions.conclusion: A company's actual strategy is always a blend of proactive planned actions and reactive adaptive responses.

official_questions.question: Write a short note on the concept of strategy.
answer_points: In business, strategy refers to the ways an organisation responds to dynamic and often hostile external forces while pursuing its vision, mission and long-term objectives; it is incorporated to reduce uncertainty and complexity arising from environmental changes.

Strategy relates the goals of the organisation to the means of achieving them. It is management's game plan to take market position, conduct operations, attract and satisfy customers, compete successfully and achieve objectives.

It may be defined as a long-range blueprint of an organisation's desired image, direction and destination — what it wants to be, what it wants to do, how it wants to do things and where it wants to go. It provides an integrated, unified framework for mobilising resources, directing human effort and handling opportunities and threats.

Strategy is flexible and pragmatic, enabling adaptation to environmental changes and unforeseen situations; it integrates goals, policies and actions into a cohesive whole for survival, growth and competitive advantage.

It may be formulated at corporate, divisional and functional levels; corporate-wide strategies are operationalised by divisional and functional strategies. A company's strategy is typically a blend of proactive actions and reactive responses to unanticipated developments.
keywords: dynamic and often hostile external forces

official_questions.question: Novatek Electronics Ltd., a smart home appliance maker, planned to expand into Tier-2 cities, invest in AI-enabled products, strengthen its dealer network and increase exports. During implementation a foreign competitor launched low-priced products, raw material prices rose and stricter energy-efficiency rules came in, so the company launched budget products, changed suppliers and accelerated energy-efficient product development. Explain how this case shows that strategy is partly proactive and partly reactive.
answer_points: The case combines deliberate plans with responses to unforeseen developments.

**Proactive strategy:** expanding into Tier-2 cities, investing in AI-enabled products, strengthening the dealer network and increasing exports are planned initiatives to achieve long-term objectives and build competitive advantage.

**Reactive strategy:** in response to unexpected changes (a low-priced foreign competitor, rising raw material prices, stricter energy-efficiency rules), Novatek introduced budget variants, changed its sourcing and accelerated energy-efficient products — actions to address emerging challenges.
official_questions.conclusion: An organisation's realised strategy is a blend of proactive (deliberate) actions and reactive (adaptive) responses: proactive strategies achieve planned objectives, reactive ones help adapt and sustain competitive position.

official_questions.question: You are a strategic consultant to a retail company facing increasing competition from online retailers. Using the concept that strategy is partly proactive and partly reactive, explain how the company can develop a strategic approach to this challenge.
answer_points: The company can develop an approach that is both proactive and reactive.

**Proactive strategy:** proactively analyse market trends and customer preferences to identify growth opportunities — e.g. invest in market research to understand what customers value in a retail experience and tailor offerings. This helps stay ahead of competitors and attract new customers.

**Reactive strategy:** be prepared to react to market changes — e.g. if a competitor launches a new online shopping platform, quickly assess the impact and develop a response. This helps adapt to changing conditions and maintain competitiveness.
official_questions.conclusion: Combining proactive and reactive strategies gives a comprehensive approach: capitalise on growth opportunities while mitigating risks and responding to threats.
keywords: assess the impact and develop a response

official_questions.question: ABC retail chain regularly tracks consumer trends to adjust its offerings and keeps a flexible supply chain to respond swiftly to demand fluctuations, enabling it to anticipate market shifts and adapt to them. Which type of strategy is the retail chain employing?
answer_points: The retail chain combines proactive and reactive elements.
Monitoring consumer trends and adjusting offerings shows a **proactive** approach to anticipate and meet customer needs.
Maintaining a flexible supply chain to respond quickly to changes in demand reflects a **reactive** strategy to address unforeseen market shifts.
This dual strategy lets the chain anticipate future trends and react effectively to immediate changes, ensuring competitiveness and customer satisfaction.
official_questions.conclusion: Its strategy is partly proactive and partly reactive.

mcqs.explanation: Keeping ahead to reap first-mover advantages is a planned, deliberate move to improve market position: a proactive strategy (SM §1.3). ICAI key: (C).

mcqs.question: Primo Neo Logistics saw its airways business decline, wants to study rivals' market positions and then modify its strategy to adapt to changing circumstances, while also planning to use its resources and capabilities to grow through new means of transport and a collaboration. The strategy being followed is:

options.D: Blend of proactive and reactive strategy

mcqs.explanation: The facts show both planned growth initiatives (proactive) and modifying strategy in response to declining business and competition (reactive). A company's strategy is typically a blend (SM §1.3). ICAI key: (D).

why_wrong.B: Ignores the adaptation to the decline.

mcqs.trap: Picking 'adaptive' because the case says 'adapt'.

mcqs.question: Alex Motor Company anticipated future urban mobility needs and launched a hybrid vehicle for congested cities, after sales had declined and critics called it outdated. Strategic management allowed the company to be:

options.A: More directive towards the cross-functional team to reduce communication barriers
options.B: Partly proactive, as it anticipated future urban mobility needs, and partly reactive, as it responded to declining sales
options.C: More proactive, as it readily launched a new vehicle with updated technology
options.D: More authoritative in taking faster decisions

mcqs.explanation: Anticipating future mobility needs is proactive; responding to falling sales and criticism is reactive. ICAI key: (B).

why_wrong.A: Not a strategic-management benefit shown in the facts.
why_wrong.C: Ignores the response to declining sales.

mcqs.trap: Option C sounds right but is only half the picture.

mcqs.question: A mid-sized electronics firm notices a rapid rise in demand for smart home devices and redesigns its product line to cater to this trend while competitors are still hesitant. Which strategic approach is the firm using?
mcqs.explanation: Acting ahead of competitors on an emerging trend is a planned, proactive move. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: The firm acts before competitors, not in reaction to them.
why_wrong.D: The firm is changing its product line.

mcqs.trap: 'Notices demand' may suggest reaction, but acting while rivals hesitate is proactive.

mcqs.question: Royal Pens, facing a fall in market share due to emerging competitors, launched Bluetooth-enabled styluses and limited-edition pens. These were not pre-planned innovations but responses to market shifts. What type of strategic approach is this?
mcqs.explanation: Actions taken in response to market shifts rather than pre-planned are reactive (adaptive) strategy. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.C: A competitive-strategy label (SM Ch 4), not the approach asked.

mcqs.trap: New products tempt you to say proactive.

mcqs.question: Zenith Global Enterprises' renewable energy SBU secured a $500 million contract with a European government for solar power solutions. This decision is an example of:

options.B: Proactive expansion into international government partnerships
options.C: Reactive change based on customer feedback

mcqs.explanation: Seeking and winning a new international contract is a planned move to improve market position: proactive. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: No uncertainty is being reacted to.

mcqs.trap: None — look for the planned initiative.

mcqs.question: A retail chain notices that competitors have introduced same-day delivery. In response, it quickly adjusts its logistics and ties up with local couriers to match the offering and avoid losing customers. What type of strategy is it implementing?
mcqs.explanation: Matching a competitor's move after it happens is an adaptive reaction to changing circumstances: reactive. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.C: Logistics is functional, but the question asks the strategic approach.

mcqs.trap: Option C is partly true but not what is asked.

mcqs.question: Kriti Pvt. Ltd., importer of French cheese brand Fromage, regularly attends industry conclaves and reads business magazines. Sensing that the growing 'Vocal for Local' sentiment could hurt its French brand, it partnered with local producers of traditional Indian cheeses. Which action is an example of a proactive strategy?

options.A: Selling off its French business assets
options.B: Responding to the 'Vocal for Local' sentiment by partnering with local cheese producers
options.C: Managing customer relations and nationwide distribution
options.D: Covering all marketing expenditures for Fromage in India

mcqs.explanation: The company anticipated a shift in sentiment through environmental scanning and acted before its brand was disrupted — a planned move to improve its position. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: A funding step for the new plan, not the strategic initiative.
why_wrong.D: Done by the French affiliate under the existing deal.

mcqs.trap: The word 'responding' — here the response comes before the damage, from anticipation.

concepts.title: 1.4–1.4.1 Strategic Management and Its Importance
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (May 2024 Q5(b), Jan 2026 MCQ 14) · RTP 3 · MTP 4
understand: ==The importance of strategic management lies in enabling an organisation to perform better than its competitors and its own past and present performance== — superior returns to investors, superior value to customers, and superior performance against the expectations of employees, suppliers, government and society.

==The overall objectives of strategic management are two-fold: (1) to create competitive advantage (something unique and valued by the customer), so that the company can outperform competitors in all aspects of performance; (2) to guide the company successfully through all changes in the environment, i.e. to react in the right manner.==

Operations are strongly influenced by the **increasing rate of change** in the environment and its ripple effect. Changes may be external or introduced by managers, and may appear as blurring of industry and firm boundaries driven by **technology, deregulation or globalisation**. Crafting, implementing and executing strategies are the **heart and soul** of managing a business.

**Meaning:** ==strategic management refers to the managerial process of developing a strategic vision, setting objectives, crafting a strategy, implementing and evaluating the strategy, and finally initiating corrective adjustments where deemed appropriate.== The process does not end; it keeps going in a **cyclic manner**. It involves developing the vision, **environmental scanning (external and internal)**, strategy formulation, implementation, and evaluation and control.

Originally called **business policy**, strategic management emphasises monitoring and evaluating **external opportunities and threats in the light of the company's strengths and weaknesses**, and designing strategies for survival and growth.

**Importance (§1.4.1).** Formulating and implementing strategies are essential for survival and growth in a turbulent environment. **'Survival of the fittest' (Charles Darwin)** applies: the 'fittest' are not the largest or strongest but those that **change and adapt successfully**. Giants that failed to manage drastic change include **Bajaj Scooters, LML Scooters, Murphy Radio, BPL Television, Videocon, Nokia and Kodak**.

Business follows the war principle of **'win or lose'** (win-win only in a few cases), so each organisation must build competitive advantage, which can be done only through strategic management: strategic analysis, formulation and implementation, evaluation and control.

**Major benefits:** (1) gives **direction** to move ahead — helps define goals and mission and realistic objectives in line with the vision; (2) helps organisations be **proactive instead of reactive** in shaping their future — analyse and act instead of being mere spectators, control their own destiny, work within the vagaries of the environment and shape it; (3) provides **frameworks for all major decisions** — businesses, products, markets, manufacturing facilities, investments, organisational structure — and guidance on what the organisation is trying to achieve; (4) **prepares the organisation to face the future** and acts as a **pathfinder** to opportunities; (5) serves as a **corporate defence mechanism against mistakes and pitfalls**, avoiding costly mistakes in product-market choices or investments; (6) **enhances the longevity** of the business — a clear stand in the industry, not surviving on luck ('actions over expectations'); (7) helps develop **core competencies and competitive advantages** for survival and growth.

The importance lies in **superior (above-average) organisational performance**. But in search of meaning and purpose, organisations may take decisions that are **not strictly 'strategic'** yet worthy on their own: belief in diversity, inclusion and equity; improving availability, affordability and accessibility of products to opportunity-deprived sections; greater workplace democracy.

answer_points: **Level:** Raghav's role represents the **functional level** of strategy — his responsibilities focus on crafting and executing marketing and sales strategies that drive customer engagement and competitive positioning.

Strategic management helps Elvis Global **define its goals and mission**, giving clear direction so marketing efforts align with the overall vision and Raghav can set realistic objectives supporting long-term goals.
Raghav can **proactively shape the future** rather than merely react to market changes — anticipate trends, manage environmental uncertainties and stay ahead of competitors.
It provides a **robust framework for critical decisions** on marketing strategies, target markets and resource allocation, ensuring coherent and consistent decisions aligned with business objectives.
It helps **identify and exploit new opportunities** — campaigns that resonate with emerging preferences — so Elvis Global can differentiate itself and gain market share.
It acts as a **defence mechanism against mistakes and pitfalls** in marketing decisions and campaign execution, giving a structured approach to identifying and mitigating risks.
It **enhances longevity and sustainability** by keeping marketing strategies adaptable and resilient and giving a clear position in the industry.
It enables **core competencies and competitive advantages** — strong brand identity, innovative content, superior customer service.

concepts.title: 1.4.2 Limitations of Strategic Management
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (May 2025 MCQ 14, May 2026 Q8(b)) · RTP 4 · MTP 9
understand: ==The presence of strategic management cannot counter all hindrances and always achieve success.== The limitations are:

**(1) Environment is highly complex and turbulent.** It is difficult to understand and pinpoint how it will shape up; the organisation's estimate of the future may awfully go wrong and **jeopardise all strategic plans**. The organisation deals with suppliers, customers, governments and other external factors, so ==relying on a business strategy blindly could go absolutely wrong if the environment is turbulent==. Example: two-wheeler EV brands counted on strategic benefits from the government's push for electric mobility, but customers became reluctant due to safety concerns over battery fires — strategy cannot overcome a turbulent environment.

**(2) Strategic management is a time-consuming process.** Organisations spend a lot of time preparing and communicating strategies, which may **impede daily operations** and negatively affect routine business. Planning matters, but success lies in action; too much time on planning and formulating may not be fruitful (like students spending so much time planning what to study that they are exhausted before studying).

**(3) Strategic management is a costly process.** It adds a lot of expenses: expert strategic planners must be engaged, and effort goes into analysing environments, devising strategies and implementing them. This is really costly for organisations with limited resources, particularly **small and medium organisations**; experts are costly resources.

**(4) Difficult to estimate competitive responses.** Where all organisations move strategically, it is difficult to estimate competitors' responses because their decisions are taken **behind closed doors** by top management. Example: Apple removed the 3.5 mm audio jack from iPhones, and all major speaker brands had to develop true wireless speakers (TWS) and compete with new entrants.

**Why businesses still opt for strategic management:** it is time-consuming and costly, but ==its importance outweighs its shortcomings==; a business cannot operate and succeed without proper strategic management.

**ICAI case pattern (Ramesh Sharma / Vikram Patel):** a store owner who manages strategically still loses sales to online stores. ICAI's answer applies each limitation: complex, turbulent environment (a new kind of competitor); difficulty predicting the future; time-consuming, but he should continue managing strategically; costly, but he may engage experts for customised offerings; small stores cannot visualise how large online players will move strategically.

answer_points: **Overall objective:** (1) to create competitive advantage so that the company can outperform competitors; (2) to guide the company successfully through environmental changes and react in the right manner.

**(1) Complex and turbulent environment:** the environment is highly dynamic and uncertain; estimates about future conditions may go wrong and affect strategic plans adversely. Strategy cannot always overcome a turbulent environment.
**(2) Time-consuming process:** extensive planning, analysis and communication may impede daily operations and routine activities; excessive planning may reduce execution efficiency.
**(3) Costly process:** expert planners, environmental analysis and implementation efforts increase costs, especially for small and medium enterprises.

**(4) Difficulty in predicting competitive responses:** in a competitive environment it is difficult to estimate competitors' strategic actions accurately, as such decisions are generally confidential and uncertain.

concepts.title: 1.5 Strategic Intent (Vision, Mission, Goals, Objectives and Values)
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (Jan 2026 MCQ 9) · supports every vision / mission / objectives / values question in this chapter
understand: ==Strategic management is a dynamic process of formulation, implementation, evaluation and control of strategies to realise the organisation's strategic intent.==

Senior managers must define **"what they want to do"** and **"why they want to do"**. =="Why they want to do" represents the strategic intent of the firm.== Clarity in strategic intent is extremely important for future success and growth, **irrespective of the nature and size** of the enterprise.

Strategic intent can be understood as the **philosophical base of strategic management**. It implies the purposes an organisation endeavours to achieve; it is a statement that provides a **perspective of the means** which will lead the organisation to reach its vision in the long run. It gives an idea of what the organisation desires to attain in future and answers **what the organisation strives or stands for**. It indicates the **long-term market position** the organisation desires to create or occupy and the opportunity for exploring new possibilities.

Strategic intent provides the **framework** within which the firm adopts a predetermined direction and operates to achieve strategic objectives. It could be in the form of **vision and mission statements at the corporate level**, and expressed as the **business definition and business model at the business level**.
Strategic intent is generally stated in **broad terms**, but when stated in precise terms it is an expression of aims to be achieved operationally, i.e. **goals and objectives**.

**Components (SM list):** **1. Vision** — blueprint of the company's future position; describes where the organisation wants to land; depicts aspirations and a glimpse of what it would like to become; every sub-system must follow it. **2. Mission** — delineates the firm's business, its goals and ways to reach them; explains the reason for the firm's existence in society; helps potential shareholders and investors understand the firm's purpose; identifies 'what business the firm undertakes'; defines present capabilities, activities, customer focus and role in society. **3. Goals and objectives** — the base of measurement: goals are end results the organisation attempts to achieve; objectives are **time-based measurable targets** that help accomplish goals; in practice no distinction is made and the terms are used interchangeably. **4. Values / value system** — deep-rooted principles guiding an organisation's decisions and actions.

The **vision, mission, business definition and business model explain the philosophy** of the organisation, while **goals and objectives represent the results** to be achieved in multiple areas of business.

While strategic intent is the **purpose** an organisation aims to achieve, ==values form the omnipresent foundation of every decision management takes==. An organisation without values is like an organisation with no real intent.
**SM figure (Component of Strategic Intent):** Strategic Intent → Vision → Mission → Goals and Objectives, with **Values / Value System** at the centre of all of them.

concepts.title: 1.5.1 Vision
understand: Very early in strategy making, senior managers must consider **what directional path** the company should take and what changes in its **product-market-customer-technology focus** would improve its current market position and future prospects. Committing to one path pushes managers to draw carefully reasoned conclusions about how to modify the company's business make-up and the market position it should stake out.

==Top management's views about the company's direction and the product-customer-market-technology focus constitute the strategic vision for the company.== ==Strategic vision delineates management's aspirations for the business, providing a panoramic view of 'where we are to go' and a convincing rationale for why this makes good business sense.==

Strategic vision thus **points out a particular direction, charts a strategic path to be followed in future, and moulds organisational identity**. A clearly articulated strategic vision **communicates management's aspirations to stakeholders** and helps **steer the energies of company personnel in a common direction**. For instance, **Henry Ford's vision of a car in every garage** had power because it captured others' imagination, aided internal efforts to mobilise the company's resources, and served as a reference point for gauging the merits of strategic actions.

**SM examples:** **HDFC Bank Ltd.** — vision of being a **world class Indian bank**, keeping 'where we want to go' central to strategic decisions. **LIC Ltd.** — 'A trans-nationally competitive financial conglomerate of significance to societies and Pride of India.' **Apple Inc. (Tim Cook)** — 'We believe that we are on the face of the earth to make great products, and that's not changing.'

==Essentials of a strategic vision:== (1) the **entrepreneurial challenge** in developing a strategic vision is to **think creatively about how to prepare a company for the future**; (2) forming a strategic vision is an **exercise in intelligent entrepreneurship**; (3) a well-articulated strategic vision **creates enthusiasm among the members of the organisation**; (4) the best-worded vision statement **clearly illuminates the direction in which the organisation is headed**.

**ICAI's added points on why vision matters (May 2025 answer):** it provides a clear sense of direction, helping the organisation focus resources and efforts on defined long-term goals; it is a source of **alignment and inspiration for stakeholders** — employees, customers and investors — by communicating the overarching purpose; and it **shapes identity and culture**, encouraging unity and collective motivation.

concepts.title: 1.5.2 Mission — and Distinguishing It from Vision
concepts.evidence: PYQ 4 (May 2024 Q7(b), Sep 2024 MCQ 13, Sep 2025 Q6(a), May 2026 MCQ 13) · RTP 6 · MTP 8
understand: ==A mission is an answer to the basic question 'what business are we in and what we do'.== Many firms fail to conceptualise and articulate the mission and business definition clearly; such firms fumble in identifying opportunities and fail in formulating strategies to use them. Firms managing strategically cannot be lax about mission and business definition, as the two ideas are **absolutely central to strategic planning**.

==Why should an organisation have a mission?== (1) To ensure **unanimity of purpose** within the organisation; (2) to develop a **basis or standard for allocating organisational resources**; (3) to provide a basis for **motivating the use of the organisation's resources**; (4) to establish a **general tone or organisational climate**, suggesting a businesslike operation; (5) to serve as a **focal point** for those who can identify with the organisation's purpose and direction; (6) to facilitate the **translation of objectives and goals into a work structure** involving assignment of tasks to responsible elements; (7) to **specify organisational purposes** and translate them into goals so that **cost, time and performance parameters can be assessed and controlled**.

==A company's mission statement is typically focused on its present business scope — 'who we are and what we do'.== Mission statements broadly describe an organisation's **present capability, customer focus, activities and business make-up**.

**SM examples:** **HDFC Bank** — two-fold mission: to be the preferred provider of banking services for target retail and wholesale customer segments, and to achieve healthy growth in profitability consistent with the bank's risk appetite. **LIC Ltd.** — ensure and enhance the quality of life of people through financial security by providing products and services of aspired attributes with competitive returns, and by rendering resources for economic development. **Apple** — to bring the best user experience to its customers through innovative hardware, software and services.

A mission statement should reflect the **philosophy of the organisation** as perceived by senior managers. ==A good mission statement should be precise, clear, feasible, distinctive and motivating.== Points useful while writing a mission: it should give the organisation its **own special identity, business emphasis and path for development**, setting it apart from similarly positioned companies; a company's business is defined by **what needs it is trying to satisfy, which customer groups it targets, and the technologies and competencies it uses and activities it performs**; good mission statements are **unique to the organisation** for which they are developed.

**What is our mission? And what business are we in? (Drucker and Levitt).** Peter Drucker and Theodore Levitt were among the first to raise this issue: as the **first step in business planning**, every firm must clarify the corporate mission and accurately define the business it is engaged in. The firm should raise and answer basic questions: What is our mission? What is our ultimate purpose? What do we want to become? What kind of growth do we seek? What business are we in? Do we understand our business correctly and define it accurately in its broadest connotation? Whom do we intend to serve? What human need do we intend to serve through our offer? What brings us to this particular business? What would be the nature of this business in the future? In what business would we like to be in future?

The **corporate mission is an expression of the growth ambition** of the firm; it is the firm's future visualised, a dramatic picture of what the company wants to become, the corporation's dream crystallised, a colourful sketch of how the firm wants its future to look, irrespective of the current position — a **grand design of the firm's future**. Mission amplifies what brings the firm to this business, what existence it seeks and what purpose it seeks to achieve; it **serves as a justification for the firm's very presence and existence** and legitimises it.

**Drucker's test — 'What business are we in?'** The answer should have a **marketing or external perspective**, not be restated in production or generic activity terms. SM table: **Indian Oil** — production-oriented: 'we produce oil and gasoline products'; marketing-oriented: 'we provide various types of safe and cost-effective energy'. **Indian Railways** — 'we run a railroad' vs 'we offer a transportation and material-handling system'. **Lakme** — 'in the factory, we make cosmetics' vs 'in the retail outlet, we sell hope'.

**Vision vs mission (ICAI answer used in MTPs):** the **vision describes a future identity** while the **mission serves as an ongoing and time-independent guide**. A vision statement can galvanise people to achieve defined objectives, even stretch objectives, provided it is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time bound. A mission statement provides a path to realise the vision in line with its values. Both have a direct bearing on the bottom line and success of the organisation. A mission statement defines the purpose or broader goal for being in existence or in business and **can remain the same for decades if crafted well**, while a vision statement is **more specific in terms of both the future state and the time frame**; vision describes what will be achieved if the organisation is successful.

**Significance of vision and mission together (ICAI answer, Sep 2025):** **Vision** — provides a blueprint of where the organisation wants to be; aligns organisational efforts on a chosen path; creates enthusiasm and moulds identity; clarifies aspirations in products, markets, customers and technology. **Mission** — explains the reason for the firm's existence; ensures unanimity of purpose and efficient resource use; is a standard for allocation and goal translation; gives distinct identity and direction; reflects present activities and ensures legitimacy.

concepts.title: 1.5.3 Goals and Objectives
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (Sep 2024 Q6(a), May 2025 MCQ 9, Jan 2026 Q8(b)) · RTP 1 · MTP 1
understand: Business organisations translate their vision and mission into **goals and objectives**. The terms are broadly synonymous, though some authors distinguish them: ==goals are open-ended attributes that denote future states or outcomes; objectives are close-ended attributes which are precise and expressed in specific terms.== Objectives are more specific and translate goals into long-term and short-term perspectives; in practice the terms are used interchangeably.

==Objectives are an organisation's performance targets — the results and outcomes it wants to achieve.== They function as **yardsticks for tracking performance and progress**. All organisations have objectives; their pursuit is an **unending process** so that organisations sustain themselves. Objectives give **meaning and sense of direction**; organisational structure and activities are designed and resources allocated **around the objectives**; they also act as **benchmarks** for guiding activity and evaluating performance.
==Objectives with strategic focus relate to outcomes that strengthen an organisation's overall business position and competitive vitality.==

==Characteristics objectives must possess to be meaningful:== (1) define the organisation's **relationship with its environment**; (2) be **facilitative towards achievement of mission and purpose**; (3) provide the **basis for strategic decision-making**; (4) provide **standards for performance appraisal**; (5) be **concrete and specific**; (6) be **related to a time frame**; (7) be **measurable and controllable**; (8) be **challenging**; (9) **different objectives should correlate with each other**; (10) be **set within the constraints of organisational resources and the external environment**.

**Need for both short-term and long-term objectives.** A company's set of financial and strategic objectives should include both. **Quarterly or annual objectives** focus attention on delivering immediate performance improvements; targets to be achieved within **three to five years** prompt consideration of what to do now to perform better later. A company aiming to double sales within five years cannot wait until the third or fourth year to start growing sales and its customer base; annual (or quarterly) targets indicate the **speed** at which longer-range targets are to be approached.

**Long-term objectives:** to achieve long-term prosperity, strategic planners commonly establish long-term objectives in **seven areas**: ==Profitability, Productivity, Competitive Position, Employee Development, Employee Relations, Technological Leadership, Public Responsibility==.

Long-term objectives represent the **results expected from pursuing certain strategies**; strategies are the **actions taken to accomplish** long-term objectives. The time frame for objectives and strategies should be consistent, **usually two to five years**.

**Short-range objectives can be identical to long-range objectives** if the organisation is already performing at the targeted long-term level (e.g. an ongoing objective of 15% profit growth every year that is currently being achieved). They differ most when managers are trying to **elevate performance** and cannot reach the long-range target in one year; then short-range objectives serve as **steps toward** the long-term objectives.

**Benefits of clearly established objectives:** they provide direction, allow synergy, aid in evaluation, establish priorities, reduce uncertainty, minimise conflicts, stimulate exertion, and aid in both the allocation of resources and the design of jobs.

concepts.title: 1.5.4 Values / Value System
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (May 2025 Q6(a), Sep 2025 MCQ 9) · RTP 1 · MTP 2
understand: Ratan N. Tata (2006, TATA Group website), quoted in the SM: "Business, as I have seen it, places one great demand on you: it needs you to **self-impose a framework of ethics, values, fairness and objectivity** on yourself at all times."

==Values are the deep-rooted principles which guide an organisation's decisions and actions.== **Collins and Porras** define core values as being **inherent and sacrosanct**; they can **never be compromised**, either for convenience or short-term economic gain. Values often reflect the values of the company's founders — **Hewlett-Packard's celebrated 'HP Way'** is an example. They are the **source of a company's distinctiveness** and must be maintained at all costs.
**Common examples of values:** ==Integrity, Trust, Accountability, Humility, Innovation and Diversity==.

**Why values are important.** A company's values set the **tone for how its people think and behave**, especially in **situations of dilemma**. They create a **sense of shared purpose** to build a strong foundation and focus on the **longevity of the company's success**. Employees prefer to work with employers whose values resonate with them. A majority of consumers say they would prefer to buy products and services from companies whose purpose reflects their own value and belief system. Hence ==values have both internal and external implications==.
During the **Covid-19 pandemic** many leaders put people before everything else, showing how deep the organisations' foundations were and how important upholding core values was.

**SM graphic:** VALUES sit at the centre of Intent, Vision, Mission and Goals & Objectives; values remain the core of all of them and of putting them into action. Vision is followed by mission, then goals, and finally execution through real actions.

**Values of HDFC Bank (SM example):** committed to the highest level of ethical standards, professional integrity, corporate governance and regulatory compliance; its business philosophy is based on **five core values: Operational Excellence, Customer Focus, Product Leadership, People and Sustainability**.

**Intent vs values (SM box).** Are values narrower than intent? No. ==Intent is the purpose of doing business, while values are the principles that guide decision-making of the business.== They go hand in hand, and intent is sometimes driven by values, so ==values are wider than intent==.

**ICAI's added points (May 2025 answer):** values are fundamental principles or standards guiding behaviour and decision-making; they are at the core of strategic intent and help define a company's **culture and ethical posture**. **Internally** they influence employee behaviour, build trust, boost morale and create a consistent workplace culture; **externally** they shape how customers, investors and society perceive the company.

concepts.title: 1.6 Strategic Levels in Organisations — Corporate, Business and Functional
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (May 2024 Q5(b), Jan 2025 Q7(a), Sep 2025 MCQ 11) · RTP 8 · MTP 12
understand: ==A typical large organisation is a multi-divisional organisation that competes in several different businesses.== It has **separate self-contained divisions** to manage each business. Example: **Patanjali** has healthcare, FMCG, organic foods, medicinal oils and herbs and other businesses, each with its own division.

Generally there are **three main levels of management**: ==corporate level, business level and functional level==. **General managers** are found at the first two levels, but their strategic roles differ with their sphere of responsibility.

An organisation is divided into segments that work together to bring a product or service to market. If a company provides several different products or services, it duplicates these functions and creates **self-contained divisions**, each with its own set of functions, to manage each product or service. The general managers of these divisions become responsible for their product line; their overriding concern is the **healthy growth of their divisions** and they decide how to create competitive advantage and achieve higher profitability with the resources and capital they have. ==Such divisions are called Strategic Business Units (SBUs).==

**Corporate level.** Consists of the **Chief Executive Officer (CEO), other senior executives, the board of directors and corporate staff**. Their role is to **oversee the development of strategies for the whole organisation**: defining the **mission and goals**, determining **what businesses it should be in**, **allocating resources** among businesses, formulating and implementing strategies that **span individual businesses**, and providing **leadership** for the organisation as a whole.

Example (SM): the **Adani Group**, a multinational conglomerate in mining, ports and airports, power generation and transmission and cement. Its Group Chairman's main strategic responsibilities are setting overall strategic objectives, allocating resources among business areas, deciding whether to divest businesses and whether to acquire new ones — i.e. developing strategies that **span individual businesses** and building and managing the **corporate portfolio** to maximise corporate profitability. It is **not** their specific responsibility to develop strategies for competing in individual business areas; that belongs to **business-level managers**.
In simple words, corporate-level managers provide an **organisation-level view** of strategy and what they want to achieve; business-level managers ensure it for their particular business.

Besides overseeing resource allocation and managing divestment and acquisition, corporate-level managers provide a **link between the people who oversee strategic development and those who own the firm (shareholders)**. ==Corporate-level managers, particularly the CEO, can be viewed as the guardians of shareholders' welfare==; it is their responsibility to ensure that corporate and business strategies are **consistent with maximising shareholders' wealth**, failing which the CEO is likely to be held accountable by shareholders.

**Business level.** A **strategic business unit is a self-contained division** with its own functions (finance, purchasing, production, marketing) providing a product or service for a particular market. The principal general manager at this level is the **head of the division**. Their strategic role is to ==translate the general statements of direction and intent that come from the corporate level into concrete strategies for individual businesses==. Corporate-level managers are concerned with strategies spanning businesses; business-level managers with strategies **specific to a particular business**.

**Functional level.** Functional managers are responsible for **specific business functions or operations** (human resources, purchasing, product development, customer service and so on). A functional manager's sphere is generally confined to **one organisational activity**, whereas general managers oversee a whole company or division. Though not responsible for the overall performance of the organisation, they have a major strategic role: to ==develop functional strategies in their area that help fulfil the strategic objectives set by business- and corporate-level general managers==.

==Functional managers provide most of the information that makes it possible for business- and corporate-level general managers to formulate realistic and attainable strategies.== Because they are **closer to the customer** than the typical general manager, they may generate important ideas that later become major strategies, so general managers should listen closely to them. An equally great responsibility at the operational level is **strategy implementation: the execution of corporate and business-level plans**.

**SM figure:** Headquarter → **Corporate strategy: where to compete?**; SBU 1/2/3 → **Business strategy: how to compete?**; business functions → **Functional strategy: how to implement business strategy?**

**Top-down or bottom-up? (SM box).** A **top-down** approach is when decisions are made solely by leadership at the top, i.e. the corporate level, while the **bottom-up** approach gives all teams across the levels a voice in decision making.

official_questions.question: Outline the main levels of management generally found in an organisation. Also explain the types of networks of relationship between these levels and amongst the same levels of a business. (3 + 2 marks)
answer_points: **Main levels of management.** In a typical large organisation there are three main levels:

**1. Corporate level:** includes the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), senior executives and the board of directors. Their primary responsibility is to oversee the organisation as a whole, make strategic decisions, define the mission and goals, allocate resources, and manage the corporate portfolio of businesses.

**2. Business level:** consists of general managers responsible for specific Strategic Business Units (SBUs). They translate corporate-level strategies into concrete plans for their divisions, focusing on creating competitive advantages and achieving profitability.

**3. Functional level:** encompasses managers responsible for specific functions such as finance, marketing and human resources. They develop functional strategies aligned with the objectives set by corporate and business-level managers and are crucial for implementing strategies effectively.

**Types of networks of relationship.** **Functional and divisional relationship:** an independent relationship where each function or division is managed independently, with business-level managers reporting to corporate-level managers (e.g. finance and marketing functions operate under their respective heads, who report to the division head).

**Horizontal relationship:** a flat structure promoting equality among all employees, facilitating openness and transparency; all positions, from top management to staff level, share the same hierarchical status, enhancing idea-sharing and innovation, particularly in start-ups.

**Matrix relationship:** a complex structure combining various departments into project-based teams, featuring multiple business-level managers for each functional team, suitable for large organisations with diverse operations.
official_questions.conclusion: These levels and their relationships streamline decision-making and strategy implementation, fostering a cohesive approach to achieving business goals.

official_questions.question: The Board of Gromax Industries Ltd., a conglomerate with six business units, discussed allocating the highest capital budget for the next five years to the most promising unit, divesting the loss-making logistics division and framing a unified dividend policy for the group. Which level of strategy is being addressed? Explain with reasons.
answer_points: The decisions represent **corporate-level strategy**.

Corporate-level strategy is formulated by top management, the board of directors or corporate headquarters, and defines the overall scope, long-term direction and resource allocation for the entire organisation.

It involves decisions on the portfolio of businesses, entry into or exit from sectors, allocation of financial resources among business units, and policies affecting the whole enterprise such as investment, growth, stability, retrenchment and dividend decisions.

Here the Board decides which unit receives the highest capital allocation, evaluates divestment of the poorly performing logistics unit and frames a common group dividend policy. These influence the future growth path, competitive positioning and overall value maximisation of the conglomerate.

Therefore they fall under corporate-level strategy, as they determine the strategic direction and structure of the company as a whole rather than individual business operations or functional activities.

official_questions.question: Swati is the marketing manager at a software company, responsible for developing and implementing marketing strategies, leading a team of marketing professionals, working with product development and sales teams, and analysing market trends and customer feedback. Which level is she working at? Discuss the roles and responsibilities of this level in the organisation.
answer_points: Swati operates at the **functional level** of management, specifically as marketing manager.

Functional managers oversee specific departments or functions such as marketing, finance or operations. Their primary responsibilities include implementing corporate strategies and policies within their area of expertise and ensuring that daily operations are conducted efficiently and effectively.

In Swati's case, the role involves developing and executing marketing strategies, leading a team, collaborating with product development and sales teams, and analysing market trends and customer feedback to refine strategies, so that products are effectively promoted and marketing aligns with overall business goals.

Functional managers bridge the gap between corporate strategy and daily operations: they translate high-level strategic goals into actionable plans for their departments and ensure effective execution.
They are often key decision-makers within their areas of responsibility, making strategic choices that affect the company's success.

official_questions.question: Although functional-level managers operate at the lower end of the management hierarchy, their responsibilities are vital for the smooth and successful functioning of a business. Discuss the importance of functional-level managers in achieving organisational objectives.
answer_points: Functional-level managers handle specific business functions such as HR, purchasing, product development, accounts, sales and customer service.
They operate at the bottom of the management hierarchy and follow the instructions and guidelines issued by business- and corporate-level managers.
Though not responsible for the organisation's overall performance, they play a major strategic role by developing functional strategies that support the strategic objectives set at higher levels.
They provide crucial operational and customer-related information that enables business- and corporate-level general managers to formulate realistic, practical and effective strategies.

Because they work closely with frontline staff and customers, functional managers gain first-hand insights that may lead to new ideas and improvements, sometimes becoming major strategic initiatives for the company.
They play an equally important role in strategy implementation, ensuring that corporate and business-level plans are executed effectively at the operational level.

concepts.title: 1.6.1 Network of Relationship between the Three Levels
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (Jan 2025 Q7(a), second part) · RTP 1 (Sep 2024) · MTP 2 (Mar 2025, Jul 2026)
understand: The **corporate level decides what the business wants to achieve**, the **business level draws ideas and plans to execute** it, and these **flow down to the functional level** to execute and achieve results. But the levels can be linked in several ways, and ==it depends on the organisation as a whole to decide what kind of network of relationship suits its culture and aspirations==.
There are **three major types of networks of relationship** between the levels and amongst the same levels of a business:

**(1) Functional and divisional relationship.** An **independent relationship** where each function or division is run independently, headed by the function/division head, who reports directly to the business head. Functions may be finance, human resources, marketing etc., while divisions may follow products — for a toy manufacturer, kids' toys, teenager toys and so on.

**(2) Horizontal relationship.** All positions, from top management to staff-level employees, are in the **same hierarchical position** — a **flat structure** where everyone is considered at the same level. This leads to **openness and transparency** in work culture and focuses more on **idea sharing and innovation**. It suits **start-ups**, where sharing ideas with speed is desirable.

**(3) Matrix relationship.** A **grid-like structure** of levels, with teams formed from people of various departments, built for **temporary task-based projects**. It helps manage **huge conglomerates** where tracking every team independently is nearly impossible. In a matrix relationship there is **more than one business-level manager for each functional-level team**. It is **complex for smaller organisations but extremely useful for large organisations**.

**ICAI's comparison table (RTP Sep 2024 answer):** Functional and divisional — benefits: specialisation, clear management of functions and products; drawbacks: potential departmental isolation, limited collaboration. Horizontal — benefits: open communication, encourages innovation and fast idea sharing; drawbacks: hard to scale, unclear roles and responsibilities. Matrix — benefits: facilitates cross-functional collaboration, flexible resource management for complex projects; drawbacks: complex reporting structures, potential conflicts.
concepts.example: MTP Mar 2025: XYZ Enterprises runs its automobile division as independent units (functional and divisional), its IT division on dual reporting to project and functional heads (matrix), and its start-up incubator as a flat team (horizontal).

official_questions.question: Tech Innovators Inc., a rapidly expanding technology company, aims to lead in artificial intelligence and machine learning and is evaluating which organisational relationship will best support its vision: the functional and divisional relationship for specialisation, the horizontal relationship for flat collaborative management, or the matrix relationship for cross-functional teams. Which will most effectively achieve its strategic goals, and why?
answer_points: The **matrix relationship** is the most effective structure for Tech Innovators Inc. to achieve its vision of leadership in AI technologies.
It promotes cross-functional collaboration, essential for managing complex AI projects and fostering innovation.

By integrating expertise from various departments into temporary, task-based teams, the matrix relationship supports dynamic project management and aligns with the company's strategic goals for advancing AI technologies.
Despite its complexity, this approach provides the flexibility and collaboration necessary for a leading-edge AI and ML focus.

Comparison: functional and divisional gives specialisation and clear management of functions and products but risks departmental isolation and limited collaboration, so it is less effective for cross-functional AI projects; horizontal gives open communication and fast idea sharing but is hard to scale with unclear roles, so it suits start-ups rather than large AI initiatives; matrix facilitates cross-functional collaboration and flexible resource management, though with complex reporting and potential conflicts, making it ideal for managing diverse, innovative AI projects.

official_questions.question: XYZ Enterprises operates in multiple industries. Its automobile division functions independently with separate teams for electric and fuel-based vehicles; its IT division follows a structure where employees report to both project heads and functional managers; and its start-up incubator lets all employees collaborate and share ideas openly regardless of hierarchy. Identify and explain the network relationships used.
answer_points: **Automobile division — functional and divisional relationship:** the division operates independently, with distinct teams handling electric and fuel-based vehicles. Each division is managed by a business-level head who reports directly to corporate-level management. This ensures clear accountability, specialisation and focused decision-making, letting XYZ cater to different market segments effectively.

**IT division — matrix relationship:** employees report to both project heads and functional managers. This allows efficient resource utilisation, as employees contribute to multiple projects while remaining aligned with their departments. The matrix relationship helps manage complex software development projects needing cross-functional expertise, ensuring collaboration among development, marketing and finance.

**Start-up incubator — horizontal relationship:** all employees, regardless of hierarchy, collaborate and share ideas openly. This nurtures transparency, quick decision-making and innovation, which are essential for start-ups where speed and adaptability matter.
By adopting these network relationships, XYZ Enterprises maximises efficiency, agility and innovation across its diverse operations.

expected_questions.question: Write a short note on the networks of relationship between the three strategic levels, and state when each is suitable.
answer_points: The corporate level decides what the business wants to achieve, the business level plans execution and the functional level executes; the organisation decides which network of relationship suits its culture and aspirations.

**Functional and divisional relationship:** an independent relationship where each function or division is run independently under its head, who reports to the business head; suitable where specialisation and clear product or function management matter.
**Horizontal relationship:** a flat structure where all positions share the same hierarchical status, giving openness, transparency and fast idea sharing; suitable for start-ups.

**Matrix relationship:** a grid-like structure with teams drawn from various departments for temporary, task-based projects, with more than one business-level manager for each functional team; complex for smaller organisations but extremely useful for large ones and conglomerates.
The choice involves trade-offs: isolation versus collaboration, speed versus scalability, and flexibility versus reporting complexity.

cases.title: Integrated Case 1 — Sanskriti Weaves Ltd.
facts: Sanskriti Weaves Ltd. runs three businesses: handloom apparel, home furnishings and a small export unit. The board, chaired by the CEO, has decided to exit the loss-making export unit, invest the proceeds in home furnishings and frame a single dividend policy for the group.
The head of the home furnishings division has been asked to decide how the division will win against imported brands. She plans premium designs and a two-year warranty.

Ms. Rao, the marketing manager, is designing a festival campaign and gathers dealer feedback that customers now want washable fabrics; she passes this to the division head, who changes the product plan.

The company's statement of purpose reads: 'We bring handcrafted Indian textiles to everyday homes at fair prices, supporting weaver families.' Its stated aspiration is 'to be the most trusted handloom brand in India by 2032'. The founders insist that no order will ever be accepted from a buyer using child labour.

questions.q: The board's decisions to exit the export unit, reallocate funds and frame a group dividend policy are taken at which level?
reasoning: Corporate-level managers decide what businesses the organisation should be in, allocate resources among businesses and set policies for the whole enterprise (SM §1.6).
Divestment and acquisition decisions are specifically listed as corporate-level responsibilities.

questions.q: The division head's plan to beat imported brands with premium designs and a warranty is:
reasoning: Business-level managers translate corporate direction into concrete strategies for their business and decide how to create competitive advantage (SM §1.6 figure: business strategy = how to compete).

questions.q: Ms. Rao's role in passing customer insight upward illustrates which point from the study material?

options.A: Functional managers provide most of the information that lets business- and corporate-level managers formulate realistic strategies
options.B: Functional managers set the mission and goals of the organisation
options.C: Functional managers are guardians of shareholders' welfare
options.D: Functional managers decide the corporate portfolio

reasoning: SM §1.6: functional managers are closer to the customer and provide most of the information that makes realistic, attainable strategies possible; their ideas may become major strategies.

questions.q: 'To be the most trusted handloom brand in India by 2032' and 'We bring handcrafted Indian textiles to everyday homes at fair prices' are respectively:
reasoning: A statement of desired future position is the vision; a statement of present business scope, customers and purpose is the mission (SM §1.5.1 and §1.5.2).

questions.q: Explain how the founders' refusal to deal with buyers using child labour fits into strategic intent, and why such principles matter to the company.
questions.answer: It is a core value — a deep-rooted principle that guides decisions, sits at the centre of strategic intent and can never be compromised for short-term gain.
reasoning: Values are the deep-rooted principles which guide an organisation's decisions and actions; Collins and Porras describe core values as inherent and sacrosanct, never compromised for convenience or short-term economic gain.
Values sit at the centre of strategic intent: intent, vision, mission and goals are all put into action through values.
Internally, values set the tone for how people think and behave, especially in dilemmas such as a profitable order from an unethical buyer, and create a sense of shared purpose supporting longevity.
Externally, values shape how customers, investors and society perceive the company; most consumers prefer companies whose purpose reflects their own beliefs.
Values are wider than intent: intent is the purpose of doing business, while values are the principles guiding how that business is conducted.

cases.trap: The same case carries vision, mission, values and all three levels; read what each question asks for.

cases.title: Integrated Case 2 — Bharat Cycles Pvt. Ltd.
facts: Bharat Cycles has sold sturdy, low-priced bicycles for 30 years. Three years ago its planners forecast a shift to premium fitness cycles and began developing a geared model, investing in R&D while rivals waited.

Last year an imported e-bike brand entered suddenly with aggressive pricing, and a new state rule required BIS certification for imported parts. Bharat Cycles quickly changed suppliers and launched a budget e-bike.

The company spends heavily on annual strategy retreats. The finance head complains that planning consumes weeks of management time and that consultants' fees are large for a mid-sized firm, and that no one could predict the imported brand's pricing move.
Its objectives for next year are: raise revenue by 12%, cut warranty complaints by 20% and train every dealer by March.

questions.q: Developing the geared premium model three years before rivals reacted is an example of:
reasoning: Proactive strategy is planned strategy: deliberate actions by managers to improve the company's market position and financial performance (SM §1.3).

questions.q: Changing suppliers and launching a budget e-bike after the import entry and the new rule is:
reasoning: Reactive strategy is an adaptive reaction to changing circumstances — here an unanticipated competitor and a regulatory change (SM §1.3).

questions.q: The finance head's three complaints (time, cost, unpredictability of rivals) correspond to which part of the chapter?
reasoning: SM §1.4.2: strategic management is time-consuming and costly (especially for small and medium organisations) and it is difficult to estimate competitive responses.

questions.q: The targets of 12% revenue growth, 20% fewer complaints and dealer training by March are best described as:

options.B: Objectives, because they are concrete, specific, measurable and time-framed

reasoning: Objectives are performance targets that are concrete and specific, related to a time frame and measurable and controllable (SM §1.5.3).

questions.q: The managing director asks whether the company should stop investing in strategic management given the finance head's complaints. Advise him.
questions.answer: No. Continue managing strategically: the limitations are real but the importance outweighs the shortcomings.
reasoning: The presence of strategic management cannot counter all hindrances or always achieve success; its limitations are a complex and turbulent environment, a time-consuming process that may impede daily operations, a costly process (a real burden for small and medium organisations) and difficulty in estimating competitive responses, which are decided behind closed doors.
However, its importance outweighs its shortcomings: a business cannot operate and succeed without proper strategic management.

Benefits visible in this case: it gives direction and defines goals and mission; it made the company proactive rather than reactive (the geared model); it provides a framework for major decisions on products and markets; it prepares the firm for the future and acts as a pathfinder to opportunities.
It also serves as a corporate defence mechanism against costly mistakes, enhances longevity and helps build core competencies and competitive advantage.
Practical advice: continue strategic management but control its cost and time, since challenging times demand more effort, and use experts selectively to understand customer preferences.

cases.trap: The cost and time complaints tempt you to recommend abandoning strategic management; ICAI's answer is always to continue, because importance outweighs shortcomings.

descriptive.question: "Strategy is partly proactive and partly reactive." Discuss, and explain why an organisation needs both.
answer_points: A company's strategy is typically a blend of proactive actions to improve market position and performance, and reactions to unanticipated developments and fresh market conditions.
Proactive strategy is planned strategy; reactive strategy is adaptive reaction to changing circumstances.
Crafting a strategy involves stitching together a proactive/intended strategy based on prior successful experience and then adapting pieces of successful reactions as circumstances change.

Both are needed because: proactive strategies achieve planned objectives and build competitive advantage; reactive strategies cope with uncertainty from competition, technology, regulation or customer preferences; together they give flexibility and adaptability and ensure survival.
descriptive.conclusion: The realised strategy is always a blend of deliberate and adaptive elements.

descriptive.question: A newly appointed CEO of a diversified group asks what her strategic role will be. Identify her level and outline its duties and responsibilities.
answer_points: The CEO operates at the corporate level, which consists of the CEO, senior executives, the board of directors and corporate staff.
Oversee the development of strategies for the whole organisation; define the mission and goals.
Determine what businesses the organisation should be in; allocate resources among the different businesses.
Formulate and implement strategies that span individual businesses; provide leadership for the organisation.
Ensure corporate and business-level strategies are consistent with maximising shareholders' wealth; manage the divestment and acquisition process.
descriptive.conclusion: Corporate-level managers, particularly the CEO, are the guardians of shareholders' welfare.

descriptive.question: Explain the significance of a mission statement for an organisation.
answer_points: A mission statement is focused on the present business scope — who we are and what we do — describing present capability, customer focus, activities and business make-up.
It ensures unanimity of purpose; develops a basis or standard for allocating organisational resources; provides a basis for motivating the use of resources.
It establishes a general tone or organisational climate suggesting a businesslike operation; serves as a focal point for those who identify with the organisation's purpose and direction.

It facilitates translation of objectives and goals into a work structure with assignment of tasks; specifies organisational purposes so that cost, time and performance parameters can be assessed and controlled.
